summary: Gives implementation requirements and usage guidance for cryptographic algorithms in IPsec ESP and AH. The goal is to keep IPsec interoperable while letting it use up-to-date cryptography. It replaces RFC 7321 and is updated by RFC 9395.

eli5.summary: A list of which secret-code recipes IPsec programs must know, so all of them can talk to each other.

questions: which crypto algorithms for esp and ah
which encryption algorithms must ipsec support
why is manual keying discouraged in ipsec
subtitle: Which encryption, authentication and compression algorithms IPsec implementations must, should or must not support.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs cryptography that stays secure as algorithms age, while implementations from different vendors and versions still have to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists algorithms for ESP and AH with requirement levels (MUST, SHOULD, MAY, MUST NOT and graded variants) and explains each change from RFC 7321, favoring authenticated encryption.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8221 replaces RFC 7321 and is itself updated by RFC 9395, so check that document for later changes.

today: RFC 8221 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7321 and is updated by RFC 9395, which can change some of the levels given here.

sections.title: Purpose and How Requirement Levels Change
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, RFC 4303) and the Authentication Header (AH, RFC 4302) apply cryptographic protection to data sent over an IPsec Security Association. RFC 8221 gives guidance so they can use up-to-date algorithms while IPsec stays interoperable. The choice of mandatory-to-implement algorithms was moved out of the main IKEv2 specification into a separate document like this one so it can be updated more often.

The RFC aims to name the mandatory algorithm of tomorrow ahead of time, and expects changes to be gradual: an algorithm is normally downgraded from MUST to MUST- or SHOULD rather than straight to MUST NOT. Algorithms listed in the IANA registry but not mentioned here MAY be implemented. The levels also take account of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, which are resource-constrained; entries marked IoT apply to those devices and to server-side implementations that must interoperate with them.

The document gives recommendations for implementations, not for users, whose choices follow their own security policy. Only IKEv2 parameters are considered, and IKEv1 is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The rule book says which recipes cooks must know. It changes slowly, so a recipe goes from required to optional before it is banned, and kitchens have time to catch up.

sections.title: Requirement Levels Beyond RFC 2119
sections.content:
Besides the usual BCP 14 key words, the RFC defines extra levels that signal where an algorithm is heading.

SHOULD+
Same as SHOULD, but likely to be promoted to MUST at some future time.
SHOULD-
Same as SHOULD, but may be deprecated to MAY in a future version.
MUST-
Same as MUST, but expected to stop being a MUST in a future document. It is reasonable to expect it to stay at least SHOULD or SHOULD-.

The label IoT marks levels that exist for interoperability with IoT devices.
sections.eli5: Plus and minus signs are like arrows on a road sign: this rule is getting stricter, or this one is about to get looser.

sections.title: Manual Keying and Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
Manual keying SHOULD NOT be used. Without a keying protocol such as IKE, IPsec offers no Perfect Forward Secrecy, and nothing refreshes session keys, keeps Security Parameter Index values unique or ensures nonces, initialization vectors and counters are used only once. If it is used anyway, counter-mode algorithms (ENCR_AES_CTR, ENCR_AES_CCM, ENCR_AES_GCM, ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305) MUST NOT be used, which particularly affects IoT devices with no state across reboots. At the time of writing ENCR_AES_CBC is the only mandatory-to-implement encryption algorithm suitable for manual keying.

Encryption without authentication is not effective and MUST NOT be used. There are three ways to get both:

  • ESP with an AEAD cipher. This is the fastest and most modern method; the AEAD cipher is the encryption algorithm and the authentication algorithm is none (for example ENCR_AES_GCM_16 or ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305).
  • ESP with a non-AEAD cipher plus an authentication algorithm, for example ENCR_AES_CBC with AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256. It is slower because the data is processed twice.
  • ESP with a non-AEAD cipher plus AH for authentication. This is NOT RECOMMENDED: it is the slowest, and the double header lowers the effective MTU.
sections.eli5: A locked box is useless if anyone can swap what is inside, so every locked box also needs a tamper seal. The best boxes do both jobs in one step.

sections.title: ESP Encryption Algorithms
sections.content:
The table of encryption algorithms sets these levels: ENCR_NULL, ENCR_AES_CBC and ENCR_AES_GCM_16 are MUST; ENCR_AES_CCM_8 and ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 are SHOULD; ENCR_3DES is SHOULD NOT; ENCR_DES_IV64, ENCR_DES, ENCR_BLOWFISH, ENCR_3IDEA and ENCR_DES_IV32 are MUST NOT. For AES the levels apply to 128-bit and 256-bit keys, while 192-bit keys remain MAY. Because IPsec sessions can be long-lived, 256-bit keys were raised from MAY to MUST.

Algorithms IANA has allocated codes for but the IETF never specified (marked UNSPECIFIED) MUST NOT be implemented for IPsec, and neither MUST algorithms not expected to secure IPsec (marked non-IPsec). Several older, little-used ciphers became MUST NOT.

Notable decisions: ENCR_NULL stays MUST so that ESP can provide authentication only, which is preferred over AH because of NAT traversal. ENCR_AES_CBC stays MUST for interoperability, but the industry is moving to AEAD and it is expected to be replaced in the long term. ENCR_AES_GCM_16 moves from SHOULD+ to MUST to favor authenticated encryption. ENCR_AES_CCM_8 moves from MAY to SHOULD for IoT interoperability only. ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 is SHOULD because there were not yet enough ESP implementations for SHOULD+, and it is expected to become MUST in the long term. ENCR_3DES drops from MAY to SHOULD NOT.
sections.eli5: Some old secret codes have been cracked or never caught on, so they are banned. A few modern ones that lock and seal in one step are now required.

sections.title: Authentication and Compression Algorithms
sections.content:
Authentication algorithms matter for authenticated-only traffic (ESP with NULL encryption, or AH) and for non-AEAD encryption. The levels: AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 is MUST; AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96 is MUST-; AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256 is SHOULD; AUTH_AES_XCBC_96 is SHOULD for IoT and MAY otherwise; AUTH_AES_128_GMAC and AUTH_AES_256_GMAC are MAY; AUTH_HMAC_MD5_96, AUTH_DES_MAC and AUTH_KPDK_MD5 are MUST NOT. AUTH_NONE is MUST only with the authenticated encryption algorithms of the previous section and MUST NOT otherwise, down from MAY in RFC 7321.

AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 is MUST to replace AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96. Because of a long-standing common bug that truncates its hash to 96 bits instead of 128, implementations that also have AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256 are recommended to prefer it. The GMAC algorithms should only be used for AH, not ESP. Combining ESP with NULL authentication and AH is NOT RECOMMENDED, since some configurations have been shown insecure.

Compression was not covered in RFC 7321. Because it is not widely deployed it stays optional: IPCOMP_DEFLATE, IPCOMP_LZS and IPCOMP_LZJH are MAY, and IPCOMP_OUI is MUST NOT.
sections.eli5: The tamper seals get the same treatment: the weak, broken ones are banned, a strong newer one is required and an even stronger one is suggested.

sections.title: Summary of Changes from RFC 7321
sections.content: The RFC closes with a table of the status changes from RFC 7321. In short, the push is toward authenticated encryption and away from SHA-1, 3DES and unauthenticated modes. It also notes that ENCR_AES_CTR stays at MAY because it is not mentioned in the sections above.
sections.eli5: A short list of which recipes moved up, which moved down and which stayed put since the last edition of the rule book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security depends on the strength of the algorithms and keys, and also on the engineering and administration of the protocol around them. The algorithms listed as MUST or SHOULD are not known to be broken, and research to date suggests they will likely stay secure for the foreseeable future, but not necessarily forever, so the RFC expects revisions from time to time. It requires no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Today's required codes look safe, but codes get cracked over time, so the list will be rewritten now and then.
